title: Confidence intervals as procedures
dek: A 95% confidence interval is a random set with a coverage claim. Today’s endpoints are numbers; the 95% lives on the procedure.
story: A confidence interval is a set-valued estimator C(Y) such that P_θ(θ ∈ C(Y)) is at least (or approximately) 1−α for each θ in a class. After you observe y, the set C(y) either covers or it does not. There is no remaining random 95% attached to that particular interval unless you switch to a posterior.

Wald: θ̂ ± z_{1−α/2} se. Score (Wilson, for binomial) inverts a test that uses null variance. Profile likelihood intervals invert an LRT. They agree in regular large samples and quarrel when events are rare or parameters sit near a wall.

In TB screening papers, a Wald interval for a sensitivity estimated from 8 culture-positive cases will happily go negative or above 1. That is the procedure talking, not the biology. Use a score or profile interval, or a Beta posterior with a named prior.
deep: Duality: a 1−α interval is the set of θ₀ not rejected by a level-α test of H₀: θ = θ₀. Change the test (Wald, score, LRT) and you change the interval. This is why “the” 95% interval does not exist.

Coverage can be conservative or liberal at finite n. Clopper–Pearson binomial intervals are conservative; some approximate methods undershoot near 0. Simulation from the model you claim is the adult coverage check.

Nuisance parameters: a Wald interval for ψ uses a se that already plugged in λ̂. A profile interval maximises λ at each ψ. They are first-order equivalent and can differ for variance components and ratios.
Do not caption a confidence interval as “95% probability that π sits here” in a frequentist methods section. If you want that sentence, write a prior and a posterior.

formulas.label: Wald interval
formulas.note: Uses alternative-variance (observed) se. Can violate bounds of Θ.

formulas.label: Profile likelihood interval
formulas.note: Invert the LRT. Respects the shape of ℓ, including skew.

visual.caption: Coverage is a property of many hypothetical repetitions (left idea), not a probability tag on one printed interval (right idea). The bars are schematic: a well-calibrated procedure versus a Wald procedure that undershoots near a boundary.

example.title: Binomial interval for Xpert sensitivity
example.setup: 8 culture-positive pulmonary TB cases, 7 detected by NAAT. Estimate Se = 7/8 = 0.875. Compare Wald versus a bounded interval.

steps.title: Score / Wilson
steps.body: Inverting the score test keeps the interval inside (0,1) and uses p(1−p) under the candidate p, not only at p̂. The numeric interval is still wide — n = 8 is the story.

steps.title: What to write
steps.body: “7/8; 95% score interval …” plus the case definition. Do not advertise 87.5% as a stable programme constant.

example.takeaway: Coverage is about the recipe. Near 0 or 1, change the recipe before you change the biology.

check.prompt: After the data are in, a realised 95% confidence interval:
choices: Contains θ with posterior probability 0.95 by definition
Is a fixed set; the 95% referred to the procedure’s coverage, not a remaining lottery ticket on this set
Must include the MLE and the prior mode
check.answer: Is a fixed set; the 95% referred to the procedure’s coverage, not a remaining lottery ticket on this set
check.why: That is the frequentist ontology. If you want a remaining probability, use a posterior.

whyWrong.Must include the MLE and the prior mode: A CI need not involve a prior; some intervals can even exclude an MLE in odd constructions, though Wald includes it.

check.prompt: Wald 95% interval for a mean, θ̂ = 10, se = 2, z = 1.96. Endpoints nearest:
On the coverage small-multiples, what does the short Wald bar at π=0.05, n=20 mean?
choices: Wald intervals are shorter therefore better
The Wald procedure’s actual coverage fell below the nominal 95% in that rare-event regime
Score intervals do not contain π̂
Coverage is a Bayesian probability in both bars
check.answer: The Wald procedure’s actual coverage fell below the nominal 95% in that rare-event regime
check.why: The y-axis is schematic coverage percentage. A short bar is undercoverage, the usual Wald failure near 0.

whyWrong.Wald intervals are shorter therefore bet: The bar is coverage, not width.
